catalog_quote: A phonological word (hereafter, P-word) is marked by a primary stress ('). Primary stress occurs on the first syllable of P-words. If the first syllable of P-words is V, then the second syllable can be nearly as prominent as the first one. In addition to this, if the P-word which begins with a V syllable consists of two or three syllables, then the primary stress can occur on the second syllable. (These examples are W1 & W3) In reduplicated and compound P-words a secondary stress occurs on the first syllable of the second root. In simple P-words a secondary stress tends to occur on the third syllable. new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the first syllable of the phonological word ('kindau 'to plant', 'miyapo 'many', 'ahirahai 'food', 'himi`yama 'woman'). Words that begin with an onsetless vowel syllable are the exception: their second syllable is nearly as prominent, and in such words of two or three syllables primary stress may sit on the second syllable (a'ni 'I', i'kisai 'sunfly').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress (`) on the first syllable of the second root in reduplicated and compound words ('kahai`tse 'sister', 'aitse`pundai 'quick', 'huwori`hawori 'be unsteady in one's steps'); in simple words it 'tends to occur on the third syllable' ('himi`yama 'woman').
new_statements.exceptions: V-initial (onsetless) words: second syllable nearly as prominent, and in 2-3-syllable V-initial words primary stress can be on the second syllable. The earlier 1979 version (p. 8) marked stress before the second syllable in all four of its examples (a'ni, a'ku, ki'ndeu, miya'po) and said P-words 'are normally pronounced with light stresses on the final syllables with slight rising pitches'; the 1981 paper explicitly revises this section and re-marks kindau and miyapo as initial-stressed. The 1992 OPD leaves its stress heading empty.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement (phonological word, examples in isolation, including compounds and reduplications). Above the word the authors posit a phrase-final 'heavy stress' (") with rising pitch on the last syllable of the phonological phrase and sentence-level pitch contours; the 1981 paper states that the heavy stress 'is a distinctive feature seen in the higher levels than the P-word level'. In the 1979 paper (p. 7) a primary stress is also said to be placed on the first syllable of the last constituent of the phrase because of that phrase-final heavy stress. Stress is defined as 'peak of intensity' (1979, p. 2); nothing is said about contrastiveness. Description covers the eastern dialect (Yubanakor village).
new_statements.identity_note: The Manabe manuscripts describe the eastern of the two principal Kwanga dialects (about 4,000 speakers in eight villages), with data gathered in Yubanakor village (1979 ms., p. 1). Yubanakor/Daina is listed by Ethnologue/Wikipedia as a Kwanga dialect; Glottolog 5 dialect nodes under kwan1278 that I could see are Apos apos1239, Bongos bong1290, Tau tauu1239, Wasambu wasa1246 (no separate Yubanakor code found in our Glottolog CSV). Assign at language level kwan1278. Note the Glottolog record 319699 dates the Tentative Phonology 1985 (52 pp.); the SIL archive dates the same manuscript October 1979 (49 pp.), and the 1981 revision that carries the stress rule is not in Glottolog at all.
